# Mid-Sprint Check-in: @ab-wm
## Question 1: What did you implement so far in the sprint, and what remains?
So far, I have one issue (#56) that has been closed and its PR (#96) merged in. I have one issue that will be tentatively closed with the eventual merge of PR #97. Since the first issue was a medium issue worth five points, and the second issue a medium with 3 points, I decided to implement another small issue to reach a total of 10 points.

The last issue, which adds more shortcut behaviors, has actually already been implemented and its PR drafted, but this is on a completely separate git-worktree in the specstory folder. This is because I wanted to wait for the merging of the PRs before I created a new branch. Once the PR #96 is merged into main, I will cherry pick those commits into a new branch, which conviniently gives me an another chance to review the changes in each commit.

There is nothing else of note that is left to be done, other than ensuring my AI-logs have been uploaded, the links to them are updated, and any other things I may have forgotten.

## Question 2: What is ont thing you learned about the codebase or about software engineering practice?
The backend changes for the first medium sized issue I implemented really showacased the extent to which the code has been fragmented and responsibility spread everywhere. Previous to the implementation, every implementation of a shortcut had to be specifically defined at every location that it wanted to be used. Thus, there was no way to cleanly monitor clashes, the same shortcut keys kept getting implemented over and over in different places, and no central location to register or monitor the behavior of shortcuts. After the implementation, there is finally a central location through where the behavior is established and processed.

When it comes to the concept of software engineering itself, the use of AI really forced me to reckon with what is needed and what is not. Issue splitting and ACs were too specific / complicated, and feature implementations added more changes that were needed. Controlling AI meant me unknowingly following the YAGNI ("You aren't gonna need it", part of extreme programming) concept to direct the AI agent to implement features to the defined extent, reduce side-effecting behavior, and be realistic on requirements and the end goals of an issue.

## Question 3: What is one thing you would do differently?
I am not too sure how to respond to this question. A major part of my workflow has been established through the exprience from the previous sprints, such as how I control my AI agents. how I frame my PR's and issues, how do I review changes that AI implements e.t.c. I have managed to make this as efficient as possible that I would have 2 agents running at the same time doing different tasks, speeding up my efficiency.

If there is one aspect I would like to improve, that would be organizing my work. I use two different devices, and since I do not sync anything about claude to the cloud, I do not have access to the same agents that worked on a certain concept. This is a problem, as many of these agents have 100ks of tokens of context and is better suited to answer follow up problems (like reviews). It is often the case that a review overblows an issue, or make assumptions of requirements, and an agent that is already familiar with the implementation is better suited to answer it. I am looking into seeing if I can expose my home device to the internet, safely, so I can ssh into it so I can have access to those agents.
=== docs/sprint2/checkin/CarsonRackley.md
# Sprint 2 Mid-Sprint Check-in: Carson Rackley (@CarsonRackley)

## What I have done so far, and what remains

I have not completed much implementation yet. Between coursework for other classes, the in-class
presentations and Quiz 2, the first half of the sprint went mostly to planning. I read through the
whole Sprint 2 page and mapped each deliverable to what I owe: two medium issues, a peer-reviewed
spec and at least one design decision with two alternatives per issue, PRs with a Tech Debt
section, AI logs, and UML diagrams. I then updated our shared Claude context files
(`.claude-students/COURSE-WORKFLOW.md`) with the Sprint 2 rules, formats and deadlines, so anyone on
the team can ask Claude which deliverables are still missing.

What remains is most of the sprint's work. I need to choose my two medium issues and put them on
the Sprint 2 milestone, tighten their descriptions and acceptance criteria, and get each spec
peer-reviewed before I write code. Then I implement both with tests, review a teammate's PR, and
draw the class and sequence diagrams (D6) for one of my issues.

## One thing I learned

The biggest thing I learned is how differently Go organizes code compared to the Java I wrote in
Software Dev. Go has no classes. Instead, data is kept in simple structs, and functions are
attached to them separately. Rather than one class inheriting from another, Go builds bigger pieces
by placing one struct inside another, so it reuses that struct's fields and behavior. Interfaces
also work differently: in Java you have to declare that a class implements an interface, but in Go
anything that has the right functions fits automatically. That is how Gitea can use one shared
database helper to look up many different kinds of data. The web pages are built from templates
that the server fills in with data before sending them to the browser. At first this made the code
hard to follow because I kept looking for classes that weren't there. Once I understood the
pattern, tracing my Sprint 1 notification changes through the code became much easier, and I feel
more confident jumping into unfamiliar parts of the codebase.

## One thing I would do differently

I would start earlier. I let this sprint's work get pushed behind other deadlines, so now most of
it lands in the second week, along with the stress of knowing it is still waiting. Even small steps
in the first few days, like picking my issues and posting their specs, would have helped, because
peer review needs turnaround time that I cannot compress at the end. Going forward I plan to set
aside time early in each sprint just for getting my issues set up.

For the project itself, I would be more exploratory when choosing and sizing issues. Before
committing to one, I want to trace the code it touches first (models, routes, templates and tests)
so I know whether it needs a migration or spans several layers. That gives a more honest estimate,
keeps an issue from turning out bigger than it looked, and means I understand the whole
implementation before I start coding instead of discovering it halfway through.

# Mid-Sprint Check-in: @controlled-opposition

## Question 1: What did you implement so far in the sprint, and what remains?

I've implemented #65, the Playwright regression suite for dropdowns. The tests check that the issue label picker and the navbar menus set `aria-expanded` and the related ARIA attributes correctly as they open and close. PR #105 is open and waiting for a teammate review. While writing these tests I found a real bug: the label picker keeps `aria-expanded="true"` after Escape closes it. I filed it as #104 and marked that test with `test.fail()` so the suite stays green until the bug is fixed.

Three issues remain. #57 (medium) adds a `?` shortcut that opens a help dialog listing every registered shortcut. #95 (small) makes `r` quote the selected text into the reply box. #60 (small) lets users turn character-key shortcuts off, following WCAG 2.1.4. All three build on the shortcut registry from #56, which merged on 10-19. I'll do #57 first because #60 depends on it, and my UML diagrams will cover #57.

## Question 2: What is one thing you learned about the codebase or about software engineering practice?

Writing tests against what the user can observe found a bug that the existing tests had missed. Screen readers rely on the label picker's `aria-expanded` attribute, and no test checked it after Escape. The picker looked closed on screen but still reported itself as open. A test that only checked visibility would have passed. From now on, when I test an interactive widget, I'll assert the attributes assistive technology reads as well as what appears on screen.

I also learned how to keep a known bug from blocking work. If I'd left the failing assertion in place, CI would have gone red for everyone until someone fixed #104. If I'd deleted it, the bug would have been forgotten. `test.fail()` records the bug in the suite and leaves the build passing. When someone fixes #104, that test will start to fail, and that tells them to remove the marker. The bug stays documented and has a check waiting for the fix.

## Question 3: What is one thing you would do differently?

I would start the dependent issues earlier. I picked up #57, #60 and #95 on 10-18, and all three depended on #56, which hadn't merged yet. I waited for that merge instead of starting work, so halfway through the sprint I have one PR open and three issues with no code. I could have branched off the #56 branch and rebased once it merged, or started with the parts that don't touch the registry, such as the help dialog's markup or the text-selection logic for `r`.

I'd also install fewer skills in my AI setup. Every skill I add puts its name and description into the agent's context at the start of each session, so dozens of them use up context before I've asked for anything. Having so many also confuses the agent. Several skills overlap, so it sometimes loads one that doesn't fit the task, or follows instructions from two skills that disagree. I'm going to go through my skills, remove the ones I rarely use, and keep a short list that matches how I work on this project.

Closes #14

## What changed

The milestone page (`/{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}`) now has a burndown chart above the issue list, folded under a "Burndown" heading that collapses. It shows:

- **Remaining:** open items at the end of each day, stepping on the day each change happened.
- **Total in milestone:** a dashed line with ▲ where items were added and ▼ where they were removed. The milestone's first day of work is its plan, so it is not marked.
- **Ideal:** a straight line from the first day with work down to zero on the due date.
- **Projected finish:** a dotted line extrapolated from the net burn rate over the last 14 days. A one-line summary says in words whether that is early, on the due date or late, or why there is no projection yet.
- **Hover details:** hovering a day lists the items that changed on it (closed, reopened, added, removed; a merge counts as closed). The same list appears under the chart with a link to each item, since links can't be clicked inside a canvas tooltip. It starts on the latest day with changes.
- **Include pull requests:** a checkbox, off by default, kept in the page URL as `include_pulls=1` without disturbing the issue list's own filters.

History is rebuilt from timeline comments (milestone changes, closes, merges and reopens), not from the current state. There is no schema change and no migration. The chart loads from its own endpoint, `GET /{owner}/{repo}/milestone/{id}/burndown`, so the issue list stays as fast as before.

## Why

A milestone page shows only a progress bar, so there is no way to tell whether a milestone is on track, when scope changed, or when it will finish. Acceptance criteria, in the order the issue lists them:

- **AC1** (chart with actual and ideal lines): the remaining and ideal lines. The axis runs from the first day to whichever is latest of today, the due date and the projection.
- **AC2** (history rebuilt from timeline events): each item's milestone, close, merge and reopen comments are replayed. Issues migrated in without those comments fall back to their row, and the replay always ends on the database's current state, so today's count matches the progress bar.
- **AC3** (scope additions and removals marked): ▲ and ▼ on the total line.
- **AC4** (projection shown only with enough data): hidden with under two days of history, when nothing has burned down over the window, when the work is done, or when the milestone is closed.
- **AC5** (hovering a day lists what changed): in the tooltip, and repeated with links under the chart.
- **AC6** (pull request toggle, off by default, in the URL): `include_pulls=1`; the checkbox reads it on load and writes it on change.
- **AC7** (edge cases): no due date hides the ideal line and says why; a changed due date uses the current one; an overdue milestone runs to today; a closed milestone ends on its close date (or on a later change, so the last point still matches the counters); an item added already closed widens the total but not the remaining count; an empty milestone shows a message instead of a chart.
- **AC8** (no access without permission, nothing private leaked): the endpoint sits in the same route group, with the same guards, as the milestone page. The milestone pages let in anyone who can read issues *or* pull requests, so the server counts and lists a kind only if the viewer can read it, and the checkbox is hidden from viewers who can't read pull requests.
- **AC9** (strings in `locale_en-US.json`): every visible string is under `repo.milestones.burndown.*`.
- **AC10** (unit tests for replay, toggle, ideal and projection): see below.

Deliberate differences from the issue's wording:
- The ideal line starts on the **first day with work**, not the creation day. Otherwise a milestone created empty and filled the next day draws a flat line at zero.
- A due date more than a year past the chart is not drawn. The test fixtures' year-9999 due date would otherwise flatten the chart.

## How it was tested

- **Go unit tests** (`models/issues/milestone_history_test.go`, `services/issue/milestone_burndown_test.go`):
  - The calculation is a pure function that takes `now` and a time zone, so 23 table cases cover every replay path: scope creep, items leaving, reopen, merge, an item added already closed, each fallback for missing history, the database winning when comments disagree, both closed-milestone endings, late, early and windowed projections, and the ideal line's limits.
  - Every case also asserts that the last point matches the items' current state.
  - Separate tests cover the per-day change lists, and dates across the New York daylight-saving changes.
  - The query tests check that only this milestone's and repository's history is read, that events come back in order, and that the batched lookups return every row.
- **Integration tests** (`tests/integration/milestone_burndown_test.go`):
  - `RealLifecycle` closes, reopens and moves issues through the real API and checks the history records Gitea actually wrote. The final counts alone can't show that, because the replay ends on the database's state either way.
  - `PullRequestsOnRequest` checks the toggle.
  - Two tests switch off the issues unit or the pull request unit and check that nothing of that kind is counted or listed. Both were confirmed to fail when the permission check is removed.
  - The rest check not-found and private-repository access.
- **Vitest** (`RepoMilestoneBurndown.utils.test.ts`): the summary sentence, ideal and projection lines, scope markers, axis range, tooltip lines, URL handling for the toggle (the issue list's filters survive it) and item links.
- **E2E** (`tests/e2e/milestone-burndown.test.ts`): the chart renders with its summary and accessible label; a closed issue appears in the change list with the right link; the toggle starts off, writes the URL, survives a reload and clears; the chart collapses and expands; an empty milestone shows its message.
- **Checked by hand,** because canvas drawing and multi-day history can't be produced through the API in real time: screenshots against a synthetic two-week history (markers, tooltip contents, step timing, the change list while moving the pointer to it), in light and dark themes, open and collapsed.

## CI / manual verification

Run locally on the branch after merging `main`:

- `go build ./...`, `go vet`, and golangci-lint v2.12.2 for Linux and for Windows (`gogit`) on the changed packages: 0 issues.
- `go test ./models/issues/ ./services/issue/`: pass under `TZ=UTC` and `TZ=America/New_York`.
- `go test -run 'Milestone|CloseReason' ./tests/integration/`: pass.
- `pnpm exec eslint`, `stylelint`, `vue-tsc`: clean. `pnpm exec vitest run`: 57 files, 307 tests pass.
- `GITEA_TEST_E2E_FLAGS='--project=chromium tests/e2e/milestone-burndown.test.ts tests/e2e/milestone.test.ts tests/e2e/repo-issues-chart.test.ts' make test-e2e`: 5 passed. Firefox e2e times out on this machine for existing tests too, so it was not used as a signal.
- `./.claude-students/check.sh`: ok (34 docs, guide 34/34).

## Design

See the Design Decision in #14: history is rebuilt from timeline comments when the chart is requested, rather than stored as daily snapshots. Later changes are listed under Why.

Claude Code (Opus 5.5, `claude-opus-5-5`) studied the codebase, wrote the implementation plan, and wrote the code, tests and course-doc updates. It also ran the checks above and took the screenshots. When I asked whether the issue was complete, it found that the first version missed three acceptance criteria (scope markers, hover details and the pull request toggle); I had it add them, along with the collapsible chart. I chose the scope and the design decisions, approved and made every commit, merged `main`, and pushed. AI log: see the AI Assistance comment on the linked issue.

# Mid-Sprint Check-in: @arjunsb26

## Question 1: What did you implement so far in the sprint, and what remains?

My main work so far is #14, the milestone burndown chart, which was carried over from Sprint 1. PR #77 merged on 10-09. The milestone page now draws a burndown with an ideal line and a projected finish date. It marks where scope was added or removed, and hovering over a day lists the items that changed on it. A checkbox, saved in the URL, adds pull requests to the chart. The history is rebuilt from timeline comments, so it needed no migration. The PR has Go unit, integration, Vitest and e2e tests. After review I fixed stale responses when the toggle is clicked quickly, and a projection that was measured from the wrong day.

What remains is all of my Sprint 2 load. I have no issues on the Sprint 2 milestone yet. I need to pick two medium issues, write their specs with a design decision, get them peer-reviewed, and then implement them with Tech Debt sections. I also need to draw the UML diagrams for one of them, file my AI logs, and review a teammate's PR.

## Question 2: What is one thing you learned about the codebase or about software engineering practice?

I learned that a permission check on a route doesn't always mean the data behind it is safe to show. The milestone pages let in anyone who can read issues *or* pull requests, so adding my chart endpoint to the same route group was not enough. A viewer who could read issues but not pull requests would still have seen pull request titles in the chart. The server now counts and lists a kind only if the viewer can read it, and two integration tests turn off each unit and check that nothing leaks. I confirmed that both tests fail when the check is removed, because a test that never fails proves nothing.

I also learned that Gitea's timeline comments work as an event log. Replaying them lets you rebuild the past without storing daily snapshots, but the replay has to end on the database's current state. Otherwise the chart can disagree with the progress bar right above it.

## Question 3: What is one thing you would do differently?

I would check my work against the acceptance criteria before calling it done, not after. When I asked the AI whether #14 was complete, it found that the first version had missed three criteria: the scope markers, the hover details and the pull request toggle. Adding them late meant a second round of commits, more tests and another merge from main. If I had kept the criteria list open as a checklist while I worked, I would have caught those gaps on the first day.

I would also start my Sprint 2 issues sooner. Finishing #14 took the first part of the sprint, and I put off choosing new issues until it merged. That leaves the spec reviews, which depend on teammates' turnaround, crowded into the second week. Writing the specs while #14 was in review would have kept both moving at once.
